content: Niacin does not appear to influence the hepatic synthesis of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL), nor does it affect the fecal excretion of fats, sterols, or bile acids. Niacin extended-release tablets USP (film-coated) contain niacin, which, at therapeutic doses, acts as an antihyperlipidemic agent. Niacin, also known as nicotinic acid or 3-pyridinecarboxylic acid, is a white crystalline powder that is highly soluble in water. In the body, niacin is converted into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) within the NAD coenzyme system. At gram doses, niacin (but not nicotinamide) reduces total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and triglycerides (TG), while increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). The extent of these lipid and lipoprotein changes may vary depending on the severity and type of underlying lipid abnormality. The increase in HDL-C levels is associated with an elevation in apolipoprotein A-I (Apo A-I) and a redistribution of HDL subfractions. This redistribution includes an increase in the HDL2:HDL3 ratio and a rise in lipoprotein A-I (Lp A-I), an HDL-C particle containing only Apo A-I. Niacin therapy also reduces serum levels of apolipoprotein B-100 (Apo B), the primary protein component of VLDL and LDL, as well as Lp(a), a variant form of LDL that is independently associated with coronary risk. Preliminary evidence suggests that niacin may induce favorable changes in LDL particle size, although the clinical significance of this effect remains to be determined. The impact of niacin-induced lipid and protein changes on cardiovascular morbidity or mortality in individuals without preexisting coronary artery disease has not been established. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated that elevated levels of TC, LDL-C, and Apo B contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. Conversely, reduced levels of HDL-C are associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis. Epidemiological studies have shown that cardiovascular morbidity and mortality are directly correlated with TC and LDL-C levels and inversely correlated with HDL-C levels. In addition to LDL, cholesterol-enriched triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, such as VLDL, intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), and their remnants, can also promote atherosclerosis. Elevated plasma triglycerides are often found in conjunction with low HDL-C levels, small LDL particles, and non-lipid metabolic risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD). However, total plasma triglycerides have not consistently been shown to be an independent risk factor for CHD. Furthermore, the independent effects of raising HDL-C or lowering triglycerides on the risk of coronary and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality remain unclear. Pharmacokinetics Absorption Niacin concentrations in the general circulation are dose-dependent and highly variable due to extensive and saturable first-pass metabolism. Following administration of niacin extended-release tablets, the time to reach maximum plasma concentrations is approximately 5 hours. To minimize the risk of gastrointestinal upset, it is recommended to take niacin extended-release tablets with a low-fat meal or snack. Single-dose bioavailability studies have shown that the 500 mg and 1000 mg tablet strengths are dosage form equivalent, but the 500 mg and 750 mg tablet strengths are not dosage form equivalent. Metabolism Niacin's pharmacokinetic profile is complex due to extensive first-pass metabolism, which is dose-rate specific and saturable at the doses used to treat dyslipidemia. In humans, one metabolic pathway involves conjugation with glycine to form nicotinuric acid (NUA), which is then excreted in the urine. There may be a small amount of reversible metabolism back to niacin. Another pathway leads to the formation of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD). It is unclear whether nicotinamide is formed as a precursor to or following the synthesis of NAD. Nicotinamide is further metabolized to at least N-methylnicotinamide (MNA) and nicotinamide-N-oxide (NNO). MNA is subsequently metabolized into two other compounds, N-methyl-2-pyridone-5-carboxamide (2PY) and N-methyl-4-pyridone-5-carboxamide (4PY), with 2PY predominating over 4PY in humans. At therapeutic doses for hyperlipidemia, these metabolic pathways are saturable, explaining the nonlinear relationship between niacin dose and plasma concentrations following multiple-dose administration of niacin extended-release tablets. Nicotinamide does not exhibit hypolipidemic activity, and the activity of other metabolites is unknown. Elimination Following single and multiple doses, approximately 60% to 76% of the niacin dose administered as niacin extended-release tablets is recovered in the urine as niacin and its metabolites. Up to 12% is recovered as unchanged niacin after multiple dosing. The ratio of metabolites recovered in the urine depends on the dose administered. Nonclinical Toxicology There is limited information available regarding the nonclinical toxicology of niacin extended-release tablets in the drug label. Clinical Studies The role of LDL-C in atherogenesis is supported by pathological observations, clinical studies, and numerous animal experiments. Observational epidemiological studies have clearly established that high total cholesterol or LDL-C levels and low HDL-C levels are risk factors for CHD.
